claims.text: Multi-component refractory high-entropy alloys have very high melting temperatures, typically above 2500 K.
The target RHEAs are disordered BCC or FCC solid solutions containing four to five principal refractory elements.
High configurational entropy can stabilize simple BCC or FCC solid solutions relative to intermetallic formation or phase decomposition.
Chemical short-range order can occur in refractory high-entropy alloys, including MoNbTaW.
Chemical short-range order influences defect or atomic mobility in high-entropy alloys.
Chemical short-range order significantly controls lattice stability and melting thermodynamics in RHEAs.
CALPHAD can rapidly screen RHEA composition spaces for phase stability and approximate melting temperatures.
DFT-trained machine-learning interatomic potentials accurately capture complex multicomponent interactions and short-range order in RHEAs.
MLIP-driven molecular dynamics can calculate RHEA melting temperatures using heating/cooling cycles or two-phase simulations.
Thermodynamic integration in MLIP-driven molecular dynamics can calculate the entropy of fusion of RHEAs.
Fluctuation formulas or direct MLIP-driven simulations can calculate the heat capacity of RHEAs.
A combined CALPHAD, DFT-trained MLIP, and molecular-dynamics workflow can accurately predict melting temperature, entropy of fusion, and heat capacity in multicomponent RHEAs.
Pure DFT is computationally prohibitive for screening vast multicomponent composition spaces.
Classical EAM or MEAM potentials often fail to represent multicomponent interactions and short-range order in RHEAs, causing inaccurate melting-property predictions.
CALPHAD alone may be inaccurate for novel RHEA compositions because its parameterization is limited by sparse experimental data.
The hybrid method is valid only for single-phase BCC or FCC RHEAs with four to five principal elements and no phase decomposition at melting.
The hybrid method may be inaccurate for multiphase alloys, intermetallic-forming compositions, or systems with unmodeled magnetic contributions.
Extrapolating an MLIP to temperatures or compositions outside its DFT training set increases prediction uncertainty.
Finite-size effects and the assumption of equilibrium melting in molecular dynamics can introduce errors or omit kinetic melting effects.
The hybrid methodology will predict melting temperatures within ±5% of experimental values.

contradictions.description: The claimed accuracy is ±5%, but the proposed experiment declares falsification only for deviations greater than ±10%. Deviations between 5% and 10% would violate the stated accuracy claim without meeting the stated falsification criterion.
